note: Wren Phonics Phase 5b (b406, 2026-10-07) — National Curriculum Year 1 'alternative sounds for graphemes' and 'alternative spellings for phonemes already known'. These are NOT new letter shapes to form (children already write every grapheme used here) — they are new SOUND mappings for a grapheme already taught (entry_type alternative_pronunciation) or new SPELLINGS for a phoneme already taught (entry_type alternative_spelling, which introduces a genuinely new grapheme). No character/mnemonic cast is used at this stage — by Year 1 the cast-and-action approach from Phases 2-4 has been retired in favour of short, direct teaching notes, matching how real Year 1 phonics moves away from early-years mnemonics. provenance: Wren original, b406, 2026-10-07.

alternative_pronunciations.teaching_note: At the end of a short word, 'y' can say the same sound as 'igh' in 'light'. Try it in: my, by, fly, cry, try, shy.

alternative_pronunciations.taught_as: /y/ as in yes, yak, yellow; also /igh/ as in my, fly
alternative_pronunciations.teaching_note: At the end of a LONGER word, 'y' usually says /ee/ instead. Compare a short word ('my') with a longer one ('happy') to hear the difference.
After a 'w', 'a' can say /o/ instead of its usual short sound. Listen for it in: was, what, want, wash, wasp, swan.
On its own at the end of a tiny word, 'e' can say its long name-sound /ee/. Try: he, me, she, be, we.
Before 'nd', 'i' often says its long name-sound /igh/ instead of the short sound. Try: find, mind, kind, behind, blind.
On its own at the end of a word, 'o' can say its long name-sound /oa/. Try: go, no, so, zero.

alternative_pronunciations.taught_as: /o/ as in dog, hot, top; also /oa/ as in go, no
alternative_pronunciations.teaching_note: Sometimes 'o' says /u/ instead of either of its other sounds — these just have to be heard and remembered. Try: son, mother, come, love, some.
After certain letters, 'u' can say the short /oo/ sound instead. Try: put, full, pull, push, bull.

alternative_pronunciations.taught_as: /u/ as in sun, cup, mud; also /oo/ as in put, full
alternative_pronunciations.teaching_note: At the start of some words, 'u' says /yoo/ — like the letter's own name. Try: unicorn, unit, uniform, universe.
Before 'e', 'i' or 'y', 'c' usually says /s/ instead of /k/. Try: cent, city, ice, fence, pencil.
Before 'e', 'i' or 'y', 'g' can say /j/ instead of /g/. Try: giant, gem, cage, stage.
In some words (often borrowed from other languages), 'ch' says /k/ instead. Try: school, chorus, echo, Christmas, stomach.

alternative_pronunciations.taught_as: /ch/ as in chip, chat, much; also /k/ as in school
alternative_pronunciations.teaching_note: In a few other borrowed words, 'ch' says /sh/ instead. Try: chef, machine, chalet, moustache.
The same two letters 'ow' can also say /oa/, like in 'go'. Try: snow, grow, own, slow, window.
In the middle of some words, 'ie' says /ee/ instead of /igh/. Try: field, chief, thief, shield, believe.
In a group of words, 'ea' says the short sound /e/ instead of /ee/. Try: head, bread, spread, instead, breakfast.
In a few words, 'ou' says the long /oo/ sound instead. Try: soup, group, you, route, youth.

alternative_pronunciations.taught_as: /ow/ as in out, loud, round; also /oo/ as in soup, you
alternative_pronunciations.teaching_note: In another small group, 'ou' says the short /u/ sound. Try: young, touch, country, double, cousin.
In some words, 'ear' says /er/ instead of /ear/ — there's no simple rule for which, so these are best learned as a small group. Try: earn, learn, early, pearl, heard.

alternative_pronunciations.taught_as: /ear/ as in hear, year, dear; also /er/ as in learn, early
alternative_pronunciations.teaching_note: 'ear' can also say /air/, the same sound as in 'chair' — in a small set of everyday words: bear, pear, wear, tear (as in tear a page). Read the word both ways and choose the one that makes sense.
Straight after a 'w', 'or' says /er/ instead of /or/. Try: word, work, world, worm, worth.

alternative_spellings.teaching_note: Four letters, one sound — 'eigh' says /ai/, the same sound already known from 'rain' and 'day'.
Without the silent 'gh', 'ei' can say the same /ai/ sound on its own.
At the end of a word, 'ey' most often says /ee/ (like 'key' or 'monkey'). In a smaller group of words it says /ai/ instead (like 'they' or 'grey') — point out both when they come up.
At the end of a word, 'ore' says /or/ — the same sound already known from 'for', spelled with a silent 'e' on the end.
A small group of words spell /or/ with 'oor' instead.
Another way to spell /or/ — say it as /or/, not as the 'ou' sound in 'out'.
